newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Land tipped for good profit growth.
newsitem.headline: HK Land tipped for good profit growth.

text.p: Hongkong Land Holdings is likely to be one of the few relatively bright spots on the Jardine group's 1996 profit horizon, analysts said.
While other companies in the Jardine stable are expected to report flat results, analysts see Hongkong Land as having had a relatively good year.

The Hong Kong-based but Singapore-listed company is 32 percent-owned by Jardine Strategic Holdings Ltd, which is 60 percent-owned by Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd. It reports its 1996 results on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley recently described the company as having "the best quality commercial property portfolio in non-Japan Asia".

"Even if Hongkong Land continues simply to collect its rents, NAV (net asset value) should rise and earnings should gradually pick up, particularly now that the millstone...of Trafalgar House has fallen from the company's neck," it said.
Hongkong Land has benefited from the sale last year of British conglomerate Trafalgar House Plc, which freed it up to focus on Asian operations, analysts said.
Janice Wallace of Goldman Sachs (Asia) said Trafalgar House had "drained" Hongkong Land, not just financially but in terms of management time.
Now the company was free to refocus on Asia and had aggressively sought new investment opportunities, she said.
"I would say that they have a new lease on life," she said.

Since Trafalgar was sold to Kvaerner last April, Hongkong Land has invested in an Indonesian toll road operator, won a tender for a commercial site in Singapore, and made its first significant property acquisition in Hong Kong in a decade.
Wallace expected Hongkong Land to report net profit of US$675 million for 1996, including the US$218 million Trafalgar exceptional, against US$257 million the previous year.
Michael Green of Salomon Brothers said Hongkong Land contributed almost 25 percent of Jardine Strategic's earnings, excluding exceptionals.
Green expected it to increase net profit to US$648 million.
James Capel analyst Vincent Luk predicted Hongkong Land would report US$440 million in net profit, excluding the Trafalgar windfall.
Luk said Hongkong Land had already been enjoying the latest up-cycle in the Hong Kong property market.

It suffered a minor setback when the U.S. computer-maker International Business Machines Corp moved out of five floors it had occupied in Exchange Square, but had subsequently re-leased half of this space, Luk said.
Exchange Square, home of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, is one of Hongkong Land's prime office properties in the heart of the territory's Central business district.
The consensus forecast in The Estimate Directory is for net profits of US$641.2 million for the year.
The company reported net profit of $445.3 million for the six months to June 30, 1996, against US$179.1 million in the same period the previous year.
